manufacturer.toshiba.description: Japanese computer manufacturer represented here by its T-series portable PCs.
manufacturer.toshiba.history:
Toshiba grew from two Japanese electrical companies: Hisashige Tanaka's telegraph-equipment workshop, begun in 1875, and Hakunetsu-sha, a lamp maker founded in 1890. Their 1939 merger created Tokyo Shibaura Denki, soon known as Toshiba. That dual heritage of heavy industry and electrical products explains why computing always coexisted with many other technologies.

Before the laptop, the company had introduced Japan's first word processor in 1978. Launched in Europe in 1985, the T1100 put an IBM PC/XT-compatible computer into a transportable 4.1 kg format with an LCD, 3.5-inch floppy drive and battery. It was not the only portable computer of its day, but Toshiba and the IPSJ museum identify it as a commercial milestone for the category.

The 1986 T3100 brought a more powerful platform to Europe and the United States, while the J-3100 series served Japan. The T-series preserved by BluMach belongs to that evolution: the T3200 and T5200 are 286 transportables with plasma displays, built to carry office capabilities that had previously required a desktop. Portable did not yet mean light; form factor, display, power and expansion supported different uses.

In 1989 Toshiba introduced Dynabook in Japan, followed by the Libretto mini-notebook in 1996. LCD panels, 2.5-inch disks, batteries and semiconductors developed within the group helped sustain this evolution. Toshiba's PC story is therefore that of a diversified company turning component and manufacturing technologies into increasingly mobile computers.
